one_liner: Three tiny x86-64 assembly memsets (GPR, SSE2, AVX2) after Microsoft's 2021 CRT design; claims 10-370% over glibc memset.
what_it_does: Provides fancy_memset_basic (64-bit GPR stores, no SIMD registers, meant for kernels), fancy_memset_sse2 and fancy_memset_avx2, each a standalone .S file with the memset(void*, int, size_t) signature and System V register usage (rdi, sil, rdx). They are not called memset by default; building with -DMEMSET=memset (the files use #ifndef MEMSET) or calling the fancy_* names is how you use them. The repo also carries a cycle-count bench (bench.c) that races them against the system memset and vendored bionic, FreeBSD and Solaris memsets, a rep stosb one-liner and a naive C loop, plus a correctness test (test.c).
how_it_is_fast: Size classes chosen with a few compares: lengths below one vector are written with two to four overlapping unaligned stores (4-byte, 16-byte or 32-byte), so there is no byte loop and no tail loop. Larger fills store one unaligned head vector, then run a 4x-unrolled loop of aligned stores (64 bytes per iteration for SSE2, 128 for AVX2) and finish with three aligned stores plus one overlapping unaligned store at the end. In the default build (erms) very large fills hand off to rep stosb after aligning the destination to 64 bytes (from 800 bytes in the SSE2 and basic versions, from 256 KiB in the AVX2 version); an ermsq build of the SSE2 version uses rep stosq from 2600 bytes.
when_to_use: A freestanding kernel, bootloader or custom libc on x86-64 that needs a small, readable memset: fancy_memset_basic uses only general-purpose registers, and each file is about 140 lines.
A static binary on known AVX2 hardware where memset is a measured hotspot for cache-resident, variable-length fills of roughly 1 byte to 4 KiB (the only range the committed bench covers).
Replacing an older generic memset (a rep stos one-liner, an old FreeBSD or bionic SSE2 routine) where the README's 20-150% and 5-100% gains apply.
As a compact reference for the overlapping-store memset design before writing your own for another ISA.
when_not_to_use: As a blanket replacement for glibc memset: the 10-370% glibc figure has no per-size table, CPU, compiler or glibc version, so whether it wins on your machine is unknown until you run bench.c.
Large or uncached fills: no non-temporal stores, and the author says the bench never touches uncached memory and that rep stos and bionic should do better there (issue #1).
Streams of mixed sizes: every timing repeats one size 100000 times with a trained branch predictor; the author lists variable-size runs as a todo.
Small constant-size memsets in ordinary code: calling a fancy_memset_* symbol stops the compiler from inlining or eliding them, which it does for memset (the README says so).
Non-x86-64 targets, the Windows x64 calling convention (the code reads rdi/rsi/rdx), or CPUs without AVX2 for the AVX2 variant (no runtime dispatch, so it faults with an illegal instruction).

integration.form: source-drop (three standalone .S files; the makefile's memset target also builds memset-basic.so, memset-sse2.so and memset-avx2.so)
integration.dependencies: none (bench and test use only libc; the optfetch submodule is not used by the makefile)
integration.min_toolchain: GNU as with .intel_syntax noprefix, driven through cc -x assembler-with-cpp (GCC or Clang); System V AMD64 ABI and ELF symbols (no underscore prefix)
integration.platforms: x86-64 only: basic needs no SIMD, SSE2 version needs SSE2, AVX2 version needs AVX2; Linux and FreeBSD mentioned (README notes AS=/usr/local/bin/as on FreeBSD); Windows x64 ABI and macOS not supported or documented
integration.thread_safety: stateless and reentrant (no globals, only argument registers and scratch registers)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same signature and return value, but exported as fancy_memset_basic/_sse2/_avx2 unless you assemble with -DMEMSET=memset, the variant must be chosen at link time to match the CPU, and ERMS use is fixed at build time

gotchas: Harness flaw in the published claims: the printout says 'higher is better' but each number is that column's cycles divided by fm SSE2's cycles, so above 1 means fm SSE2 won and the avx2 column below 1 means AVX2 beat SSE2 (issues #1 and #2; the author confirmed the inversion). The README figures were last edited in August 2021, before commit 13e5b4d (February 2022) rewrote bench.c from 5 x 1,000,000 calls on one destination (malloc+1) to 64 offsets x 100,000 calls over 1-4037 bytes, and no output from either harness is committed, so the claims cannot be tied to the current code.

ERMS is chosen when assembling: plain 'make' defines erms, so the SSE2 and basic versions switch to rep stosb at 800 bytes and AVX2 at 256 KiB; 'make erms=' removes it and 'make erms=q' gives SSE2 a rep stosq path from 2600 bytes. In the default bench the SSE2 reference column is therefore rep stosb for every length from 800 to 4037 bytes. The 'naive' column is a C loop built with gcc -O3 -fno-builtin; GCC's loop distribution can still turn such a loop into a memset call (inference, not built here).

Test coverage gap: test.c passes length l-2, so its largest case is 262143 bytes and the AVX2 rep stosb path (262144 bytes and up) is never executed; only fill values 0-3 are tested. By reading the code the path looks correct, but it is untested.

The .S files carry no .note.GNU-stack section, no .type/.size and no endbr64 or GNU property notes: linking them with GNU ld marks the stack executable (binutils 2.39 and later warn) and drops IBT/shadow-stack enforcement for the whole binary unless you add the notes or pass -Wa,--noexecstack.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick fm over nadavrot/memset_benchmark or Agner Fog's asmlib when you want a tiny, permissively licensed source-drop with a non-SIMD kernel variant and you can fix the ISA at build time; pick asmlib or AOCL-LibMem when you need runtime CPU dispatch or a whole set of string functions, and nadavrot's harness when you need glibc compared with and without PLT indirection.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README ranges only: the AVX2 version is 10-370% faster than the system glibc memset and the SSE2 version 20-150% faster than FreeBSD's and 5-100% faster than bionic's, on an unnamed CPU, compiler and glibc version, from a 2021 harness that timed one destination address. The committed bench times warm, zero-fill memsets of 1-4037 bytes at 64 destination offsets (rdtsc, 100000 calls each) and prints ratios to fm SSE2, so any AVX2-versus-glibc figure has to be derived and no results are published.
status_note: Abandoned since 2022-04-05 with one open, unanswered issue about the benchmark's inverted ratios; despite no root LICENSE file, the three memset .S files each carry a BSD-2-Clause header (Copyright 2021 Elijah Stone; commit ee040ef moved the licence into the source), so the routines are copyable, while the vendored competition files keep their own Intel BSD and CDDL terms; the README claims rest on an older harness than the committed one.
